name: kona
desc: Open-source implementation of the K programming language
why: An open-source implementation of the terse K array language, a rare and dense corner of array programming worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Kona is an open-source implementation of the k programming language, a terse, ASCII-based array language in the APL and LISP tradition. Its fundamental data construct is a list rather than APL's multi-dimensional arrays. It targets k3, an older Kx Systems version that is no longer sold, and is described as a reimplementation that is unaffiliated with Kx. You run it as an interactive interpreter from a terminal (the executable is named k), or on Windows by double-clicking k.exe.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to keep the k3 language alive after Kx stopped distributing it, since k3 has been unavailable for about 20 years. It also positions k as the preferred APL dialect for people in finance and data-heavy analysis who care about performance.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the interpreter's internals. It does say the C code deliberately imitates Arthur Whitney's terse style, and points to a 11-line buddy memory allocator by Whitney versus a roughly 750-line conventional C version as an example.

commands_seen.context: Installs Kona on macOS via Homebrew; the README's macOS route.
Clones the source repository for a build from source on macOS, Linux, BSD, Cygwin or Android.
Enters the cloned source directory before building.
Builds the interpreter from source. The README notes gmake is needed on BSD.
Starts a Kona session from the build directory.

brief.install_notes: Windows: download k.exe from the GitHub releases page and run it, or build with MinGW-w64 and MSYS/MSYS2. In MSYS, run ./k or k from the kona directory; from a native cmd window, type k, since ./k does not work there. macOS: Homebrew is the easy route. Source builds need a C toolchain and make, with gmake on BSD. Android builds use make OS=android. For input problems in the command-line interpreter, such as arrow keys showing as raw characters, the README suggests wrapping it with rlwrap. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: The C source deliberately mimics Arthur Whitney's extremely compressed style, and the README uses his 11-line buddy allocator next to a conventional 750-line version to make the point. It is also a rare, carefully scoped revival of a historical language that Kx no longer distributes.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. The project has a Travis CI badge and mailing lists, but the README shows no release dates, recent commit, or maintenance note, and I did not fetch the releases or commit pages to check.
brief.caveats: The README says the language is a reimplementation of k3 and is unaffiliated with Kx. It also says k3 has been unavailable for about 20 years, so the README does not treat it as current commercial software. Windows setup takes extra steps: MinGW-w64 and MSYS for source builds, and cmd versus MSYS run differently. The command-line interface can have input problems that the README expects you to work around with rlwrap. The license is not stated in the README I read.

entry.title: Kona
entry.tldr: An open-source reimplementation of k3, a terse ASCII array language descended from APL and LISP, run as an interactive interpreter called k.
entry.deeper_look:
Kona is an interpreter for the k programming language, specifically k3, an older version from Kx Systems. Kx no longer distributes it, and the README says k3 has been unavailable for about 20 years. Kona exists to keep that version runnable. It is unaffiliated with Kx.

The README describes k as "a synthesis of APL and LISP." Like LISP, it is ASCII-based, so you don't need a special keyboard. Its fundamental data construct is the list, where APL uses multi-dimensional arrays. The README also positions k as the preferred APL dialect for people in finance and data-heavy analysis who care about performance.

The idea underneath is array programming at extreme density: whole operations on lists expressed in a few characters, with no loops in sight. That compression carries into the implementation. The C source deliberately imitates Arthur Whitney's terse style, and the README makes the point by setting his 11-line buddy memory allocator beside a conventional C version of roughly 750 lines.

You use it as a REPL. Run `k`, type expressions, and see what comes back. It is a quick way to get a feel for a language family that most developers never meet.
entry.install:
brew install kona
# Source build (macOS, Linux, BSD, Cygwin, Android): git clone https://github.com/kevinlawler/kona.git, cd kona, make (gmake on BSD; make OS=android for Android)
# Windows: download k.exe from the GitHub releases page
# Needs a C toolchain and make only for source builds; no accounts or runtimes.

try_this.what_happens: Starts an interactive Kona session where you can type k expressions and see results.

entry.whats_unique: It is a carefully scoped revival of a historical language that its original vendor no longer distributes, written in C that imitates Arthur Whitney's famously compressed style.
entry.caveats: The README shows no release dates or maintenance note, so its current status is unclear; arrow keys may show as raw characters unless you wrap it with rlwrap, and Windows setup takes extra steps.
